text:
A former presidential adviser and senator, Babafemi Ojudu, has warned that rising political violence, ethnic suspicion and declining public confidence in state institutions threaten Nigeria’s democracy and national unity ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Ojudu called on political leaders, civil society organisations, labour unions, professional bodies, traditional and religious leaders, journalists and student groups to unite across party lines to demand a peaceful and credible electoral process.
In a statement issued on Friday, he said recent incidents of violence and attacks involving political actors and campaign teams pointed to a deeper crisis that required urgent attention.
He cited reported attacks on the campaign teams of former presidential candidates Omoyele Sowore and Peter Obi in Ado-Ekiti and Calabar respectively, as well as an alleged attack on the African Democratic Congress (ADC) campaign convoy in Kebbi State, where equipment belonging to its media crew was reportedly destroyed.
Ojudu also condemned incidents involving the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), including the disruption of its campaign visit to Lafia, Nasarawa State, where Vice President Kashim Shettima’s convoy was reportedly obstructed, and the burning of vehicles and political posters in Kankara, Katsina State.
He said all such incidents deserved investigation, irrespective of the political affiliation of those affected.
According to him, every Nigerian has the right to demand a change of government through the ballot, while every political party must be allowed to campaign peacefully.
“A citizen has every right to call for a president to be voted out. Every party has an equal right to campaign peacefully. A democracy depends on our willingness to defend both rights at once,” he said.
The former senator also expressed concern over the Federal High Court ruling in Abuja setting aside the David Mark-led leadership of the ADC and voiding the presidential nomination of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.
He noted that the party had indicated its intention to appeal the judgement, urging that the appeal be heard fairly, independently and without delay.
He, however, said the ruling raised broader questions about public confidence in the impartial application of political and electoral rules.
Ojudu warned that Nigeria’s political history offered lessons on the dangers of disputed elections and declining confidence in democratic institutions.
He recalled the disputed 1965 Western Region election, which was followed by violence and the collapse of the First Republic in January 1966, and the disputed 1983 elections, which preceded the collapse of the Second Republic in December of that year.
He also cited the annulment of the June 12, 1993 presidential election, saying the widespread support received by the late M.K.O. Abiola across regional and ethnic lines had demonstrated the potential of credible elections to strengthen national unity.
According to him, when citizens lose faith in the electoral process, the consequences extend beyond individual candidates and threaten the country’s cohesion.
“There must still be a country for whoever wins in 2027 to govern,” he said, urging presidential aspirants to explain how they intend to restore confidence in public institutions and unite Nigerians.
Ojudu said candidates should begin by rejecting ethnic incitement, defending the right of political opponents to campaign and committing themselves to accepting credible electoral outcomes.
He also said President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had a special responsibility to ensure that state institutions treated all Nigerians impartially throughout the election period.
